summary: Phoenical turns 25 years of NASA satellite fire detections into one continuous burning calendar, so ministries, municipalities and villages can see when fire season starts, when it peaks and how this year compares. Two NASA instruments, MODIS (2000 onward) and the higher-resolution VIIRS (2012 onward), see fire differently, and merging them naively creates fake jumps in the record (a 5× jump for Lebanon). We harmonize them using their 2012–2020 overlap, so a change of satellite never looks like a fire crisis. Planners get the season window, a typical-year comparison, weather at the fires and a six-month outlook, all in one place at https://www.phoenical.earth/. Wildfire planning needs history that can be trusted, and most decision-makers don’t have it.
details:
What it does: Phoenical is a web app that shows a place’s whole fire history as a “fire rings” calendar: one ring per year from 2000, one sector per month, coloured by fire-days. Around it are:

  • a 3D map of fire activity on a 0.05° grid (about 6 km), with a plain-language headline (the usual fire season, the most active year);
  • a typical-year chart (median and spread per month, with the current year overlaid);
  • weather at the fire hotspots (temperature, rain, humidity, wind) compared with the normal;
  • a six-month outlook with a likely range and its tested error;
  • a world map to pick a place, and a monthly burning digest sign-up.

It currently covers Lebanon, Greece, Portugal, Cyprus, Syria, Jordan, Turkey and the Eastern Mediterranean. It is built on global NASA data, so it can extend to other places.

How it works: NASA’s MODIS (2000 onward) and VIIRS (2012 onward) both detect active fires, but VIIRS sees far more small fires. Joining them directly makes activity appear to jump overnight (about 5× for Lebanon and 2.7× for Greece). We count fire-days per grid cell, learn the VIIRS-to-MODIS relationship over the years both satellites flew (2012–2020), and rebuild the MODIS-era record on one VIIRS-equivalent scale. After harmonization the jump at the sensor change disappears (continuity step about 1.0). We test this by fitting on 2012–2016 and checking 2017–2020, and the app shows the “VIIRS joins” marker and a MODIS raw / VIIRS raw / Harmonized switch so users can see the effect. NOAA-20 VIIRS can continue the record with a small calibration factor. The outlook is a machine-learning forecast trained on the region’s harmonized history, shown with its tested error.

Benefits: a ministry, municipality or village can see when to prepare for the season, whether this year is above or below normal, and how weather is shaping risk, without needing a GIS team. Because the record is consistent, trends such as rising activity are real and not artefacts of a satellite change.

What we hope to achieve: a trusted, shared fire calendar for every fire-prone region, so planning for the season starts before the first fire.
Repo link :https://github.com/klol120/nasa-harmonization
dataRefs: NASA FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System) active-fire detections: MODIS (from 2000) and VIIRS (from 2012), plus NOAA-20 VIIRS for continuation. We used them for the full 2000–2026 record, the sensor-overlap calibration (2012–2020) and the six-month outlook mode
